article.title: How Labor and Environmental Justice Are Uniting Against Big Coal
article.author: California DSA
article.content: Comrades on May Day 2026. Photo by Bonnie Lockhart They say history doesn’t repeat itself, but it rhymes. That’s certainly the case in Oakland these days with the return of a proposed coal depot. Back in 2015, labor organizations, environmental justice, faith-based, community, and climate activists waged a grassroots campaign and fought off plans for a coal depot at the foot of the Bay Bridge. While it seemed the grassroots organization (No Coal in Oakland) had defeated “Goliath” (the developer Phil Tagami, aka Oakland Bulk and Oversized Terminal LLC, and hedge fund operator Jon Brooks, aka Insight Terminal Solutions) with a “no coal handling and storage” Oakland ordinance, the coal industry and developers did not give up. After the city passed the “no coal storage and handling” ordinance, the developers sued the city. The case wound its way through the courts for many years until the courts ultimately ruled that the ordinance was unlawful. Once the developers prevailed, they resumed their efforts, which is when the Trump administration offered millions to resurrect the project. Now, Tagami and Brooks are once again seeking to route coal through the East Bay before it’s shipped off to Asian markets. If they succeed, Oakland, Berkeley, Richmond, El Cerrito, Albany, and Emeryville could see four or more 120-car coal trains rattling past their neighborhoods each day, spewing highly toxic coal dust en route to the rail yard in West Oakland. Why should anyone care? Well, for starters, coal dust from coal trains poses a direct threat to the health and safety of these communities. Researchers predict that, because of the toxic dust, there will be increased rates of asthma, cardiopulmonary disease, and other health conditions. Plus, burning ten million tons of coal overseas will exacerbate climate collapse. Why Did East Bay DSA Get Involved? East Bay DSA has a “No Coal in Oakland” campaign running for multiple reasons, enumerated by Cihan Tuğal in a post on the No Coal in Oakland website. Tuğal, a sociology professor at UC Berkeley and an organizer in East Bay DSA’s Climate Action Committee, said labor opposes coal because of the following: Working-class communities will suffer most from the toxic coal dust Any jobs created from the coal terminal will be short-term and hazardous, and don’t align with the broader values of creating permanent, socially responsible employment The supporters of this project are the same ones who bust unions and ultimately harm labor. “This fight is also a matter of labor pride,” Tuğal said. “The bosses want to build this terminal not just for the cash, which might be their primary motive, but also as an act of class vengeance.” He argues that the developers and their ilk say that without them, labor would be nothing because they create jobs and pay wages. But labor can join forces with social movements and environmental justice communities to enact bigger, more sustainable change. “Whenever bosses see that kind of action, they are afraid for their fundamental privileges,” he added. “That kind of victory shows that a world without oligarchs, a world where labor and communities self-consciously produce and control value, is possible. . .Ceding this turf to the oligarchs would mean abandoning our belief in a different world as much as abandoning our health and dignity.” To uphold health, dignity, and a thriving planet, East Bay DSA is saying “Keep coal out of the East Bay,” and you can too. Check out ways to get involved at www.nocoalinoakland.info .
